title: Tax banks to give some households energy bill cut, unions tell PM
description: The leader of Britain's trade unionists has told Andy Burnham the government should introduce a "social tariff", paid for by a bank surcharge, to help
body: The leader of Britain's trade unionists has told Andy Burnham the government should introduce a "social tariff", paid for by a bank surcharge, to help low and middle earners with their energy bills.A social tariff is a discount on bills based on household income, and the TUC says it believes two-thirds of households could benefit.The TUC says the bank surcharge, which was reduced in 2023 from 8% to 3% by the then Conservative government, should be reversed - and estimates it would raise £9bn over four years.TUC leader Paul Nowak said: "I think it will appeal to the prime minister. These are policies that make a difference in the real world and people can see a value in them."In a wide-ranging BBC interview ahead of its annual congress in Brighton next week, the TUC general secretary said next month's Budget needed to show "the government is back in the service of the British people".While he said Burnham had got off to a good start as prime minister, he had a series of "asks" of the prime minister and the new Chancellor, John Healey.Top of his list is more help with energy bills, saying: "We need to drive down inflation – those energy bills are fuelling inflation."And millions of families up and down the country are worried about turning on their heating this winter."Burnham has already offered "breathing space" - as he calls it – on the cost of living by temporarily scrapping VAT on electricity bills from October.Nowak said the proposal for a social tariff would be popular with Labour MPs; while the Liberal Democrats and the Greens in England and Wales have called for a windfall tax on banks too.However, UK Finance, which represents well-known banks and lenders, has suggested that heavier levies would undermine the government's ambition to deliver "growth in every postcode" and would damage international competitiveness.The organisation argues that UK banks face a heavier tax burden than those in the US, for example. So could the TUC's revenue-raising measure be counter-productive and threaten jobs in finance?Nowak is sceptical. "I can't believe banks would leave the UK just because we are restoring the surcharge to where it was in 2023. Bank share prices have risen faster here than in New York," he said.The TUC's demands for tax-raising measures don't stop with the banks, with Nowak arguing the UK has "a tax system that's good at taxing income but not good at capturing wealth".Nowak suggests a windfall tax on social media companies and for the government to equalise rates of Capital Gains Tax with income tax.The economist and former minister Lord O'Neill - who has advised Burnham – said recently that wealth taxes were "the last thing that should be happening if we want to see more growth".Nowak responded: "With respect, I think he is wrong. I'm interested in a growing economy but a growing economy that works for everybody. It is right to ask those with broader shoulders to pay a fairer share."In addition, Nowak says he doesn't believe the government will deliver on re-industrialisation and on its housing targets without making it easier to borrow to invest. As Chancellor, Rachel Reeves tweaked her so-called fiscal rules on debt and borrowing but Nowak said he believes the scope this provided for extra investment hasn't been maximised."John Healey should leave no stone unturned in allowing us to invest in our economy, in our public services and in our national security," he says."He should think about the flexibility he has got within those rules to make investments in the long term."Nowak has another ask of the government.The home secretary has announced a change in policy which would see most migrants who are in the UK wait for 10 years rather than the current five before they can settle permanently. Some care workers may have to wait 15 years.Before rejoining government Angela Rayner argued it was "unBritish" to "move the goalposts" for those already working in Britain.A consultation on the proposed measures closed six months ago, and the government is yet to produce its response.Nowak – a grandchild of migrants, from Poland and Hong Kong - says: "We should think again not just for care workers but for workers right across the board."There are 111,000 staff vacancies in social care at the moment. It's important the rules aren't changed arbitrarily. I would hope and expect this and  it needs to be the beginning of a grown-up conversation on immigration."TUC delegates will debate immigration next week and are likely to echo the call for the government to water down its changes for existing migrants.Nowak says he felt it was right for Labour to change leaders after disastrous local election results in May, and has been pleased to see a bit of a 'Burnham bounce' in the polls.And the TUC head warned the prime minister that he needs to provide "meaningful change" if he wants to see off an electoral threat from the populist Right.He says: "The onus is on Andy Burnham to show he can deliver what he promised. "If he fails to do it, there are people with glib answers who will turn this country into a more divisive place."

schema.headline: Tax banks to give some households energy bill cut, unions tell PM

title: UK needs new laws for AI in healthcare, says watchdog
description: The UK needs new regulations for AI products used in the NHS and other healthcare settings, says Britain's industry watchdog.The Medicines and Healthc
body: The UK needs new regulations for AI products used in the NHS and other healthcare settings, says Britain's industry watchdog.The Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), which regulates all medical devices and licenses treatment drugs in the UK, has published 44 recommendations to update its policies as the use of AI in the sector rises.The technology will soon be routinely used within the NHS, MHRA chief Lawrence Tallon told the BBC."What I would expect is that patients will... increasingly see AI as part of the way that normal NHS healthcare is delivered," he said."That should happen in a way that they can maintain their trust and their confidence in what's happening."The report was compiled by an independent commission and involved input from more than 12,000 people including patients and clinicians.The recommendations include:Continuously monitoring AI products and removing them from regulatory approval if they malfunction or become less effective over timeGiving patients the right to know whether AI is involved in their care, and easy access to information about the products involvedThe power to penalise the developers of an AI product if it fails to meet required standardsAn AI "L plate" system which would make it easier for new AI models to be trialled by healthcare professionals under close supervision"The medical devices regulatory framework predominantly dates from a period where we were thinking about things like hip replacements and knee replacements, or smaller things like stethoscopes and plasters," Tallon said.He added while current guidelines may work for simple AI products trained to spot known symptoms on scans, for example, the rules do not apply to more complex models."Unlike most of the medical products we're used to regulating, these products continue to change after the point of authorization," he said. "As new data gets fed in, they learn, they adapt, they drift."And he acknowledged trying to regulate AI is a global challenge."I don't think at this moment in time we can point to a single country, a single regulatory framework, and say that they have absolutely cracked it," he said.AI note-takers known as scribes, which are powered by LLMs, are reportedly used by 40% of UK-based GPs to record consultations and generate reports. But a recent study from the University of Edinburgh found patients could be less likely to share personal information such as substance abuse history if they knew the conversation was being processed by AI.Professor Henrietta Hughes, a GP who was part of the report commission, said that many of her patients were happy for AI being used during their consultations, but some chose to opt out."Some say, 'I don't want to talk to a robot', and that is also fine," she said.Prof Hughes acknowledged that the scribes could make mistakes in their notes but said it was the responsibility of doctors to correct them.While currently AI is more likely to be used to assist with administrative tasks, or carry out symptom spotting overseen by a human expert, there is a lot of excitement about its potential in the health and medical research industries.Professor Alastair Denniston, an ophthalmologist who also worked on the report, described the technology as "an exceptional opportunity" for healthcare which was "likely to rank alongside step-changes such as antibiotics and MRI".In September Rene Haas, the boss of chip designer Arm, told the BBC he believed the tech would come up with a cure for cancer "within our lifetime".But there are also concerns about AI models making wrong decisions as a result of biases in the patient data used to train them, and incorrect medical advice being given by AI chatbots.

schema.headline: UK needs new laws for AI in healthcare, says watchdog

title: Drag Race UK: BBC drops Ru Paul show after eight series
description: RuPaul's Drag Race UK is leaving the BBC after eight series, the broadcaster has confirmed.A spokesperson for the channel said it was facing "very dif
body: RuPaul's Drag Race UK is leaving the BBC after eight series, the broadcaster has confirmed.A spokesperson for the channel said it was facing "very difficult choices" in the face of "significant financial pressures".The show is currently broadcast on BBC Three and iPlayer. Future series - as well as its spin-off vs The World - will be broadcast on Wow Presents Plus, a streaming platform owned by the production company behind the show.At its peak, the UK version of the international drag competition averaged at around 1.5 million viewers per episode.A spokesperson for the BBC said it was "proud [...] of this groundbreaking show" and thanked "RuPaul, World of Wonder and everyone involved, both on and off screen".Started in 2019, Drag Race UK brought British drag into mainstream entertainment in the UK, and has made household names of drag performers such as La Voix, Danny Beard, and Tia Kofi.The show sees drag queens compete in a series of challenges to impress judges RuPaul, Michelle Visage, Graham Norton and Alan Carr, and often features big name celebrity guest judges.It has become a staple of LGBTQ+ culture and has been praised for its portrayal of the distinct style of British drag.The corporation is currently rolling out plans to make £500m of savings, with director-general Matt Brittin previously telling staff "the scale of savings requires tough choices".A BBC spokesperson said: "As the BBC continues to navigate significant financial pressures and deliver the savings required of us, we have had to make some very difficult choices, none of which have been taken lightly."Announcing the news on Instagram, Wow Presents Plus said a "new era" of Drag Race UK was on the way.A new series, Drag Race UK All Stars, which sees previous fan favourites return to compete again, will premier in Autumn 2027 exclusively on Wow Presents Plus. BBC News understands the current series of Drag Race UK, which launched in September 2026, will continue to air as normal on BBC Three and appear on iPlayer, and all existing series will continue to be available once the move is complete.The BBC declined to comment on whether future series of other international versions of the show, including Drag Race Canada and Drag Race Down Under, would continue to air.Earlier this year, the BBC announced it was dropping LGBTQ+ dating show I Kissed a Boy - which made history as the UK's first gay dating show - and I Kissed a Girl.Jordan Burrow, a contestant on series two of I Kissed a Boy, said the decision was an example of "where we're at within the queer community".The corporation said at the time that it was "exceptionally proud" of the shows but they had to make "difficult choices in light of our funding challenges".

schema.headline: Drag Race UK: BBC drops Ru Paul show after eight series

title: Apple foldable iPhone: New boss starts with gamble on latest device
description: John Ternus has entered his second week as Apple's chief executive and the company has revealed the first major change to the iPhone since it was rele
body: John Ternus has entered his second week as Apple's chief executive and the company has revealed the first major change to the iPhone since it was released almost 20 years ago.Ternus, who took on Apple's top job after Tim Cook stepped down, was onstage on Wednesday at the company's annual product release event in front of huge images of the first foldable iPhone.With a book-style format, the new iPhone, dubbed the Duo, is the largest ever size of the product. And with a US starting price of $1,999 (£1,475) going up to $3,200, it is also the most expensive. UK prices start at £1,999.Ternus said the Duo was "inspired by the iPad" but called the folding features "fluid and completely intuitive."The foldable phone has been a work-in-progress inside Apple for several years.When unfolded, the new Duo has the look of a small iPad. When folded in half, it has the look of a wider iPhone.Ternus said during the event that Apple wanted to avoid the look and feel of other foldable smart phones on the market, which he said "feel like two phones stuck together... making a larger screen feel much smaller."The Duo, he said, is the "result of a series of remarkable innovations that we think will redefine the experience of using a foldable phone."Ternus was directly involved in developing the foldable iPhone as he spent many years as a top executive inside Apple's hardware division before being tapped earlier this year as Cook's successor.Ben Wood, chief analyst at technology research firm FDM CCS Insight, said it was likely Ternus's promotion was timed specifically "to coincide with what will be arguably one of the biggest iPhone launches for many years"."Nothing happens by accident at Apple," Wood added.Carolina Milanesi, an analyst at Creative Strategies who attended the Wednesday presentation, said the spotlight on Ternus made it feel "almost like he was a product himself." Altering the design of the iPhone may address some criticism that Apple has yet to land a major product hit or truly exciting innovation since the first iPhone came out in 2007."The foldable risks becoming a premium-priced ornament in the portfolio, imparting badge value but not meaningful growth," said Dipanjan Chatterjee, an analyst at Forrester.Previously, the highest starting price of the newest iPhone was $900 (£664). Apple also revealed on Wednesday the new iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, which in the US start at $1,199 (£855) and $1,299 (£959) respectively. Chatterjee said the foldable iPhone could go the way of Apple's Vision Pro headset, which the company priced at $3,699 (£2,729) and has not been a hit with buyers. Or, he said, it could be the company's next Apple Watch which, while not as popular as the iPhone, is bought by millions of people each year.The way people have become accustomed to the way the iPhone operates is another potential hurdle to Apple seeing big sales of the new design."Foldables are interesting devices", Milanesi noted. "A lot of people are intrigued by it, but the software and the learning curve that you have from moving from a traditional phone to a foldable is real."Wood noted that the current market for foldable smartphones from the likes of Samsung and Huawei make up only 2% of smartphone sales. Even with Apple's version likely driving interest and demand, sales are only expected to reach 4% of the total market in the next decade, according to data and analytics firm FDM CCM Insight.The iPhone has been Apple's top-selling product and accounts for more than half of the company's sales each year.In recent quarters, the company has boasted that the iPhone is more in-demand than ever, with the most recent version of the device becoming its most successful product launch.The company also revealed more about the coming relaunch of its audio and chat assistant Siri, which it now calls Siri AI.Starting with the iPhone 18, the bot will now be able to go across information on a person's phone, like messages and emails, to find information, answer queries and take action on a person's behalf.Some Siri AI features will also be available on the new Apple Watch, including the ability to take notes of conversations and transcribe them, should a wearer enable that feature.Ternus referred to new AI-enabled capabilities on the iPhone as an "intelligent personal hub", and admitted that Apple would be making use of "the most private details of your daily life."He insisted that all of it will remain private, with the AI features often running "on device", meaning not through third-party companies. And when a third-party is required for a function, Ternus said it will remain private in a remote server, or cloud."Others see that data as something to collect and store", Ternus said. "Here, not even Apple can access what's yours."

schema.headline: Apple foldable iPhone: New boss starts with gamble on latest device

title: 'An injustice' or 'righting a wrong': British Jews debate sanctions move
description: From his home in the occupied West Bank settlement of Efrat, British-Israeli Rabbi Leo Dee wrote an open letter to Andy Burnham on Wednesday, accusing
body: From his home in the occupied West Bank settlement of Efrat, British-Israeli Rabbi Leo Dee wrote an open letter to Andy Burnham on Wednesday, accusing him of deciding "to single out Jewish Israelis like me for economic punishment".The rabbi's British-born wife Lucy, and their daughters Maia and Rina, were killed by Palestinians in the occupied West Bank in 2023. They were shot dead as they drove through the Jordan Valley."I am enraged at the injustice of the situation," he told the BBC, claiming the government's decision to place sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements, and not the Palestinian authority, was hypocritical.He said Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband was "living in a different universe", and argued that the main group who would face hardship as a result were the hundreds of Palestinians who were employed in them.Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the occupied West Bank by settlers since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.Miliband said the sanctions, announced after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes, were necessary to safeguard the possibility of a two-state solution - and to ensure the UK "not only calls out injustice and suffering, but acts".Rabbi Dee said he believed that, apart from a small group of "hooligan settlers" who could not be controlled and whom most people do not support, many others wanted a different outcome."Ninety-nine percent actually want to work closer with Palestinians" and have peaceful relations with them, he said, just as he did "before the 7 October attacks".Another British rabbi was also in the West Bank as the UK government made its announcement - and takes a different view.Rabbi Jonathan Wittenberg was in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair, visiting the family of Awdeh Hathaleen, a prominent Palestinian activist and English teacher who was shot and killed by an Israeli settler last year.The Emeritus Rabbi of the New North London synagogue told the BBC he wanted to show that what was happening to Palestinians there mattered to him and his community.Rabbi Wittenberg said he had "seen with my own eyes several times in the West Bank, the intimidation and threats towards Palestinians - and this needs to be called out"."It's terrible for Israel and for Israel's future, it's not what Judaism teaches and it's deeply wrong", he added.Supported by other Rabbis in the liberal and progressive UK Jewish communities, Rabbi Wittenberg believes that it is possible to support Israel, be concerned for the safety of British Jews, and that it is right for the UK government to take action to protect Israelis and Palestinians.However, he also said he was "extremely sad that it's come to this" and that he shared the "concerns of the Jewish community leadership that people will use this for antisemitism and for demonising Israel even further".Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis, who represents the Orthodox community, previously  said the sanctions marked a "truly dark day" and placed British Jews at greater risk of attacks.In Golders Green - where ambulances run by a Jewish medical charity were set on fire and two visibly Jewish men were stabbed in what police called a terror attack earlier this year - there was concern the government's actions against Israel would increase attacks against British Jews."It's so tricky because, in principle, I agree with opposing these new settlements," Michael Cohen, who works for a Jewish charity, told the BBC.But he added: "The timing of it, I think, was completely... just self interest for the Labour Party, signalling before a by-election, before the party conference."He said the practical impact of the move would be "almost zero".One woman, who runs a jewellery shop that was was twice cordoned off due to incidents in Golders Green, was very critical of the sanctions and said she would "make it my mission" to continue to buy Israeli goods whenever she could."We have to [support] our own because no one else is going to", Deborah Miller told the BBC.At the end of the week, Jewish congregations will celebrate Rosh Hashana, the Jewish New Year.Police are already increasing security around Jewish areas to protect communities who have faced multiple attacks this year and are fearful of more.The number of antisemitic incidents recorded across the UK since the start of the year is up by a fifth compared to last year, figures show.The Community Security Trust (CST), an organisation that provides security support to the Jewish community, recorded 1,926 incidents of anti-Jewish hate across the UK in the first six months of 2026.The Crime Survey for England and Wales, external, estimates that only 44% of hate crime incidents between April 2022 and March 2025 came to the attention of the police.

schema.headline: 'An injustice' or 'righting a wrong': British Jews debate sanctions move

title: August ties for hottest month on record as global heat climbs
description: Dr Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at Copernicus, described August as "a remarkable month in the global climate record", and its impacts
body: Dr Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at Copernicus, described August as "a remarkable month in the global climate record", and its impacts had been "increasingly being felt by communities, economies and ecosystems across the world".The combination of record air temperatures, record ocean heat and Europe's exceptional summer showed how climate change was now driving extremes across "both the atmosphere and the oceans", she said.World's oceans hit highest temperature on recordUN climate chief Simon Stiell said the record clearly showed humanity's impact on the climate."The evidence is irrefutable: this is the spiralling price of humanity's fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fuelling," he said.On top of the ongoing impact of the use of fossil fuels, the rise of a powerful El Niño is making matters worse, the researchers have said.El Niño is a natural climate pattern in which a band of the eastern Pacific turns unusually warm, releasing vast amounts of stored ocean heat into the atmosphere and nudging global temperatures upwards for around a year.The one currently being experienced is still strengthening and could become one of the most powerful on record, according to the Copernicus team.The biggest impact of this natural phenomenon on global temperatures is expected to hit over the coming year, meaning the current run of records may have further to go.

schema.headline: August ties for hottest month on record as global heat climbs

title: Got a migraine, acne or ear infection? Go to your chemist first
description: People will be able to go to their local chemist in England this autumn and get on-the-spot treatment for 12 common conditions without going to their
body: People will be able to go to their local chemist in England this autumn and get on-the-spot treatment for 12 common conditions without going to their GP first.Pharmacists can already prescribe medication for seven conditions -  sore throat, earache, sinusitis, shingles, impetigo, infected bites and urinary tract infections.Five more - migraines, acne, scabies, ear infections and badly blocked noses - are now also being added to that list.NHS England said the move was to ease pressure on busy GPs and A&E departments while making sure people could get treatment quickly and conveniently.After a very hot summer and three of the busiest months on record in A&Es in England, the NHS says it wants to make it as easy as possible for people to get help when they need it for everyday conditions.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said people were "fed up with the scramble for routine appointments" and wanted help close to home, with no more taking time off work or waiting to get seen."For five more common conditions, you'll be able to walk into your local pharmacy and get treated on the spot," he said.Mr Burnham said families would feel the change, and the plan would give people back "precious time".The five conditions which can now also be treated via pharmacies are:low frequency migraines in adultshay fever or allergic rhinitis in childrenear infections in adultsmild to moderate acne in young people and adultsmild skin infections and scabiesThat's in addition to these seven:sore throatsinusitisearacheinsect bitesimpetigoshinglesuncomplicated UTIsInitially, a few hundred chemists will offer treatments for the five new conditions, NHS England says.There will be a gradual rollout and the service will eventually be available at thousands of community NHS pharmacies across England.Community pharmacies also offer support with healthy eating, exercise, stopping smoking, monitoring your blood pressure, contraception, flu and Covid vaccinations.The charity the Migraine Trust said it was delighted by the news after calling for more help for migraine care in pharmacies.Chief executive Rob Music said having this support for people with migraine through their local pharmacy was "a wonderful opportunity for a faster and improved care pathway".Dr Amanda Doyle, director for primary care and community services at NHS England, said she wanted to make sure that patients can get as much support as possible in their communities, "so they do not have to be admitted to hospital unnecessarily".But bodies representing pharmacies across England have consistently said that the funding provided by the goverment does not cover the workload for the new plans."Pharmacies are still under significant financial pressures," said Henry Gregg, chief executive of the National Pharmacy Association."This shows why the government should go much further and invest in our pharmacy network that has the power to transform people's experience of everyday health issues."The Pharmacy First scheme started in England in 2024. NHS figures suggest it has delivered 14 million consultations since then, including two million appointments for sore throats and 1.7 million for urinary tract infections (UTIs).People can be referred to their local pharmacy via NHS111 or by their GP, or just go  direct to their high street chemist.Scotland has a scheme which was seen as the model for England's Pharmacy First - Northern Ireland and Wales also have systems allowing pharmacies to treat patients with certain conditions.Patients can be treated for 27 different conditions at chemists in Scotland.

schema.headline: Got a migraine, acne or ear infection? Go to your chemist first

title: Liverpool 2-1 Atletico Madrid: Alexis Mac Allister does talking on pitch
description: Liverpool will reward Mac Allister if he lets his football do talkingFigure caption, Highlights: Liverpool come from behind to beat Atletico MadridByL
body: Liverpool will reward Mac Allister if he lets his football do talkingFigure caption, Highlights: Liverpool come from behind to beat Atletico MadridByLiverpool reporter at AnfieldThe sheer ferocity of the strike to beat Jan Oblak was one thing, but the raw emotion shown by Alexis Mac Allister as he grabbed the Liverpool badge on his shirt and celebrated in front of the Kop told you all that you needed to know.Just a day earlier, Mac Allister had spoken with a different kind of emotion inside the press room at Anfield as he expressed his sadness at Liverpool not offering him a new contract during the summer. The Argentine, who is currently contracted until 2028, spoke passionately about his love for the club and the city and how he didn't feel like he had anything to prove - but there was an admittance that he needed to show the level he knew he could perform at. Thankfully for Andoni Iraola and Liverpool, Mac Allister did just that by letting his football do the talking in their 2-1 win over Atletico Madrid.From the outset against Diego Simeone's side, the midfielder seemed like a man on a mission. He blazed over early on from outside the box then picked up a booking just before the half-hour mark. Seeing Simeone wave an imaginary yellow card when he wanted a second booking for his compatriot just before half-time told a story in itself.Simeone could only watch on when Mac Allister's left foot connected with the ball from outside the box and leave a diving Oblak with no chance - turning the game on its head after Marcos Llorente's opening goal and Dominik Szoboszlai's equaliser.It wasn't quite like the strike that produced an actual seismic event - reaching a peak magnitude of 1.74 on the Richter scale - when Mac Allister found the top corner against Tottenham in 2025 on the day Liverpool won the Premier League, but it was more than good enough to beat one of the best goalkeepers in the world.And it was certainly what Iraola and the Anfield hierarchy would have wanted to see after a below-par campaign from Mac Allister last season.The understanding is that they were of the belief that Mac Allister's performances did not warrant the offer of fresh terms. But if he can carry on like this, then it will be a question of when rather than if that offer is made for whoever replaces Richard Hughes - even if Mac Allister said he didn't know if his goal would boost his chances of a new contract."It was a lovely goal from Alexis and a lovely goal from Dominik Szoboszlai. It is good the midfielders can add goals," said Iraola, who smartly navigated a question about Mac Allister's future. "We have midfielders that naturally they are going to arrive to the box - it is inside them and it is good we can also benefit offensively."Former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson said on BBC Radio 5 Live it was "exactly what Mac Allister needed to do"."If you don't get offered a new contract there's a reason, so what do you do? You go out and earn it," said Robinson."You work hard, you play to your level and he did that. He put himself about and popped up with a wonderful strike."Figure caption, How Mac Allister 'let his feet do the talking' - WarnockFive of Mac Allister's 20 goals for Liverpool in all competitions have now come from outside the penalty area.Steven Gerrard knows more than most about playing in midfield and scoring from distance for Liverpool and he described Mac Allister's performance as "outstanding"."Let your football do the talking," said Gerrard on TNT Sports. "Consistency, top performance, show your experience. Show you're a top international. This club will reward you."Mac Allister himself said how it was a "positive step" for Liverpool as they won for the first time at Anfield this season on what was Iraola's debut as a manager in the Champions League."It was a good comeback," said Mac Allister on TNT Sports. "Overall, it was a good performance. Now we have to think about the next one."Before the game we spoke about the beginning of the first half and second half. I liked the mentality."I think we showed desire today. We got the fans behind us and that's really important when you play at Anfield. A positive step for us."Figure caption, Mac Allister's brilliant finish puts Liverpool ahead'We all know the qualities he's got'Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock said Mac Allister just needed to be put into a system that suits him to get the best out of him."I don't think he has to show his importance to Liverpool, I think everyone knows the qualities he has got anyway," said Warnock, who was a pundit on Wednesday's Match of the Day."I think there will be a lot of talk about him because of what has gone on in the past few days, but I think Liverpool fans were already asking why hasn't he been offered a new contract when other players have."To come out and talk about a contract situation like he did, a couple of days before a game, and to be able to back it up the way he did with a good performance is important - but it is over the course of the season, where his performances are important because if he wants a contract and he thinks he deserves a contract then if his performances are good, he will get one."We all know the qualities that he has got - he is a World Cup winner, a Premier League winner, we know that he's a very good player, it is just he has got to be put into the right system to make it work."At the moment Liverpool's system is a little bit dysfunctional but it is starting to get better and he will get better because of that."Follow Liverpool on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical Reds contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about Liverpool

schema.headline: Liverpool 2-1 Atletico Madrid: Alexis Mac Allister does talking on pitch

title: Prince William joins Kane and Shearer in campaign to prevent suicide through sport
description: The Prince of Wales is launching a scheme that aims to use the influence of sport to help prevent suicides, with the support of sports stars including
body: The Prince of Wales is launching a scheme that aims to use the influence of sport to help prevent suicides, with the support of sports stars including Harry Kane, Kelly Holmes and Alan Shearer."Sport has the ability to reach people who may never walk through the door of a mental healthcare service," Prince William is expected to say at an event at Everton's football ground on Thursday."People who may never seek support themselves and may be struggling in silence," the prince will say later.The On Your Side project wants to give people confidence to start the "difficult conversations" with friends, relations, teammates or colleagues who might be struggling with their mental health.It aims to use the reach of sport to raise awareness about suicide and to show people the help available in a crisis, with the Football Association, Premier League and Team GB providing support.Thursday's event will be Prince William's biggest public appearance in the UK since the return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex. Earlier this week, he attended the funeral of Norway's King Harald in Oslo and brought his son Prince George to his first day as a boarder at Eton College.The level of suicide is disproportionately higher among men than women - it's the biggest cause of death for men under the age of 50 in the UK."My hope is that every sporting organisation in the country will look at what is being launched today and ask a question: 'What more can we do?' Because the opportunity before us is enormous," Prince William will say.A film has been made, featuring England football captain Harry Kane and boxer Carl Frampton, talking about the importance of stepping in and offering help if people see someone who seems to be facing mental health problems.Prince William helps to narrate the video, which aims to tackle the stigma around mental health and suicide, with 7,000 lives being lost to suicide each year in the UK.The initiative has a practical toolkit, on a free website, for people who are worried or embarrassed about what to say to someone if they have concerns about their wellbeing.It offers a sports-themed way of approaching the topic, called GOALS, representing G: get ready; O: open the conversation; A: ask the question; L: listen and respond and S: support and signpost.Alan Shearer, former England football star and TV pundit, described it as "the first suicide prevention toolkit designed for the whole of UK sport"."You don't have to be an expert. You don't have to have all the answers," said Shearer. "But we can all be better at asking, listening, and helping someone find the right support."Shearer said it was particularly poignant that the launch would be at Everton, one of the clubs where Gary Speed had played, a friend of Shearer's who died by suicide in 2011.The project has been created with mental health charities, including Chasing the Stigma, which has an app called Hub of Hope which claims to have the UK's largest mental health directory of places to get help.The charity's founder Jake Mills said he had faced his own mental health challenges and saw sport as an effective route for this type of message.He said sport was a "real force for good" in bringing people together and for "looking out for one another".Mark Bullingham, chief executive of the Football Association, said he wanted to see sports organisations "creating a culture where conversations about well-being are really encouraged. Where people feel comfortable asking for help and also know where to get it".Backing the project on Thursday in Liverpool will be former athlete Kelly Holmes, commentator Gabby Logan and former England footballer Jill Scott.Prince William has been a longstanding campaigner over mental health and preventing suicide, with his Royal Foundation having last year launched the National Suicide Prevention Network.

schema.headline: Prince William joins Kane and Shearer in campaign to prevent suicide through sport

title: Garcia vs Benn: Briton Conor Benn 'dragged down to pits of hell' by weight cut
description: Conor Benn says making the welterweight limit for his world title challenge against Ryan Garcia has felt like being "dragged down to the pits of hell"
body: Conor Benn says making the welterweight limit for his world title challenge against Ryan Garcia has felt like being "dragged down to the pits of hell" but insists he is healthy and will make weight.Benn, 29, faces WBC champion Garcia at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas on Saturday in the first world title fight of his 10-year professional career.The Briton must weigh no more than 10st 7lb (67kg) when he steps on the scales in on Friday, having not made the welterweight limit for more than four years."It's been extremely difficult," Benn told BBC Sport."It feels like I've been dragged down to the pits of hell, had a fight with Satan and God brought me back to life."Making weight has been the hardest thing I've done. I haven't made weight for four and a half years so it's going to be hard."But I won't moan when I'm getting paid a fortune to headline in Vegas for a world title. I know what I signed up for."Benn last made the welterweight limit when stopping Chris van Heerden in two rounds in April 2022.He stepped up to 11st 6lb (73kg) for two lucrative contests with Chris Eubank Jr last year, suffering the first defeat of his professional career in April 2025 before avenging the loss on points seven months later.Benn's appearance in pictures and videos posted on social media during fight week has prompted concern among some observers over the effects of dropping back to welterweight.Former world champion Carl Froch and Benn's former opponent Chris Algieri are among those to have questioned whether the weight cut could leave him depleted.It is particularly pertinent given the contrasting styles on Saturday. Benn is an aggressive, front-foot fighter who likes to apply pressure, while American Garcia, 28, possesses fast hands and is renowned for a dangerous counter left hook.But Benn dismissed concerns over his condition."I'm healthy," he said, adding that he expects to rehydrate significantly and enter the ring at around 12st 7lb (80kg) - two stones heavier than the welterweight limit.Even if he fulfils a lifelong ambition by winning a maiden world title and following in his father Nigel's footsteps, Benn intends to vacate the belt "straight away" and move back up to middleweight or potentially as high as super-middleweight."I love challenges and that's what life is about, otherwise it's boring," he added.For all the difficulty presented by the weight cut, there was little outward sign of Benn being weighed down by the occasion.He was relaxed and in good spirits as he made time for the travelling British media at the UFC's Meta Apex, with father and British boxing great Nigel Benn by his side.The former two-weight world champion has been a prominent presence throughout fight week, despite previously suggesting he would take a step back from his son's career.One man Conor Benn is yet to see, however, is his opponent.Garcia did not appear for a scheduled face-off at Mandalay Bay on Tuesday, with Benn told beforehand that the champion would not be attending.Benn turned up regardless and jokingly squared up to his 62-year-old father instead.He described Garcia as a "strange geezer" and said the no-show had done the champion "no favours"."I'm not bothered, I've dealt with worse," Conor Benn added. "If he turns up or not, it makes no difference to me."Irrespective of how hard the weight cut is or anything else, we owe it to the public to give the fans what they want. It's a lack of discipline and professionalism."

schema.headline: Garcia vs Benn: Briton Conor Benn 'dragged down to pits of hell' by weight cut

title: Wrexham couple spent £23,000 on fertility treatment but now embryos will be destroyed
description: Image source, Nat Fraser-EdwardsImage caption, Nat (left) and Nik Fraser-Edwards went through six rounds of failed artificial insemination before they
body: Image source, Nat Fraser-EdwardsImage caption, Nat (left) and Nik Fraser-Edwards went through six rounds of failed artificial insemination before they were successful through a different type of fertility treatmentByAlexandra BánfiBBC WalesNat and Nik Fraser-Edwards celebrated their son Jude's first birthday last month.After rounds of failed fertility treatment, Jude was a dream come true for the couple who said they hoped to give him a brother or sister next year. But now their dreams have come "crashing down".Their sperm donor has withdrawn his consent for further use, and the remaining five embryos in storage will be destroyed after paying £23,000 on fertility treatment.In the UK, a sperm or egg donor can withdraw consent up until the embryo is transferred into the womb.The couple now want the law changed so that once an embryo has been created, consent cannot be withdrawn.Figure caption, Nat and Nik Fraser-Edwards spent £23,000 on fertility treatment but now their embryos will be destroyedThe UK government said it sympathised and added it is "keeping all aspects of the regulatory regime under review".When they returned from their honeymoon in 2023, the couple from north Wales started fertility treatment.They took out loans and went through rounds of failed fertility treatment in a journey that cost them a total of £23,000."There was a lot of pain during that time, and everyone around us seemed to be getting pregnant," recalled Nat, 37."All you see is babies. It's not just wanting that baby so much, it's the cancelled plans in case you get that smiley face."It was only when they turned to a different type of treatment, called ICSI , where the egg is fertilised with sperm and the embryo is created outside of the body, that they had success.Nat and Nik ended up with six embryos and in August last year, Jude was born.Image source, Nat Fraser-EdwardsImage caption, Jude was born last August and Nat and Nik Fraser-Edwards (left to right) were hoping to get pregnant with their second child in January next yearThe embryos were put into storage until the couple were ready to grow their family. It was during a telephone consultation in June that they found out their embryos would be destroyed."It was very much, 'unfortunately your donor has withdrawn his consent to use your embryos'," said Nat, who lives in Penyffordd, near Wrexham."They said, 'we keep them for a cooling off period of a year and' - I think the hardest word for us was - 'we then allow them to perish'."We were absolutely floored."Nik said the couple felt "blindsided" by the fact that their sperm donor could withdraw consent at that stage."Yes, we'd signed something," she added. "But we didn't ever recall it being verbally said."Image source, Nat Fraser-EdwardsImage caption, Nat and Nik Fraser-Edwards (left to right) recently celebrated Jude's first birthday after going through rounds of failed fertility treatment. The number of donors in the UK that withdraw consent is unknown as the data isn't collected. While it is rare, it is not unheard of.Sam Beesley and Carly Estlick are expecting their first child, a boy they plan to call Finn, in October after going through IVF."I've been someone who knew from a young age that my job in life was to be a mother," said Sam, 41.Just like Nat and Nik, Sam and Carly were told last month that their sperm donor had withdrawn consent and their 10 remaining embryos will be destroyed next year."When we got the letter saying he had withdrawn consent, it felt like the wind was taken out of our sails," said Sam from Shrewsbury."We had been so focussed on the pregnancy and something going wrong, I don't think it's really sunk in yet.Image source, Sam BeesleyImage caption, Sam Beesley and Carly Estlick are expecting their first child Finn in October this year"Carly is already grieving. In her head, they've already been destroyed. Whereas until that day in 2027, I will not stop fighting."Sam said the news has put pressure on their current pregnancy."Carly is very fearful that something will happen to Finn," she said. "It has crossed my mind."I did have some reduced movements the other day and had to go to hospital. You can't help thinking, is this going to be ripped away from us as well?"This is probably our only shot at being parents. I don't know how we could afford to go through it again financially, emotionally, physically."For both couples, fertility treatment has had an emotional and financial impact.Image source, Sam BeesleyImage caption, Only last month, Sam Beesley and Carly Estlick found out they're facing the same fate as Nat and Nik Fraser-Edwards as they've been told their embryos will be destroyed in August 2027 Nat and Nik say they would have paid anything to have a family, but that the total £23,000 bill means that they did have to make "sacrifices"."We lived on the breadline for quite a while, just to make this work," Nat said. "Taking out a loan in order to pay the excessive bill."Nat and Nik also say they can't afford to go through treatment again, and, for Nik, this means she may never get to experience pregnancy."I think, as a woman, it's an amazing thing to be able to do and I didn't want to have any regrets later in life," said Nik, 36."We knew we were going to have a sibling for Jude. I think the tables turned a little bit watching Nat go through that experience and I was thinking, 'yeah I'd love to do that'."Image source, Nat Fraser-EdwardsImage caption, Nik said watching Nat carry Jude made her realise she wanted to experience pregnancy as wellThe UK fertility regulator HFEA has said that any change in the law on sperm donation is down to the UK government."It's about each person who provides an egg or sperm having that autonomy to consent and make that decision to whether they're happy for a child to be born in treatment," said Rachel Cutting, HFEA's director of compliance."Once the embryos in the uterus, in the woman's womb, there can't be a withdrawal of consent for that."The way that the law is written is that consent can be withdrawn from up to that point."We can look at it further, but it is for the law to be changed and that's not something within the power that the HFEA has. We can't change the law. But we are sympathetic to cases like this."The HFEA has said it is important that clinics warn patients of the possibility of donors withdrawing consent "because it is really upsetting and distressing when this happens".The UK government said it also sympathises with "anyone facing difficult and distressing circumstances during fertility treatment."A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: "We continue to work closely with the fertility sector to support high-quality, compassionate care, and we keep all aspects of the regulatory regime under review to the same end."If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Wrexham couple spent £23,000 on fertility treatment but now embryos will be destroyed

title: Police launch criminal investigation into Reform UK donations
description: The Metropolitan Police is carrying out a criminal investigation into Reform UK over allegations it broke foreign funding laws, following a broadcast
body: The Metropolitan Police is carrying out a criminal investigation into Reform UK over allegations it broke foreign funding laws, following a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week.An undercover reporter recorded two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations, one of which would have totalled £500,000.The police investigation by the Met's Special Enquiry Team is being folded into an inquiry that has been under way into other donations to the party.A Reform UK spokesman said the party "denies any wrongdoing and will fully cooperate with the investigation". "We won't be commenting further while a live investigation is under way."A Met spokesperson said it had received "a number of reports relating to donations and polling involving a political party", after the film by Channel 4 News and Verbatim Investigations was shown on Thursday evening. In its statement, the Met Police said: "All allegations under investigation relate to potential offences under the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000.""Detectives continue to liaise closely with the Electoral Commission and Crown Prosecution Service as enquiries progress."The police spokesperson said detectives were seeking to obtain footage relating to the broadcast.An Electoral Commission spokesperson said the Channel 4 News report included "serious allegations of wrongdoing", adding: "It is right that these are properly and thoroughly investigated by the police. "In parallel, we are also considering all relevant information and regulatory steps."The film overshadowed the party's conference in Birmingham and led to the party losing two key figures - Dan Jukes, chief of staff to the leader Nigel Farage, and James Orr, head of policy.In the news report, an undercover investigator posing as the son of an American donor is recorded raising a concern that his father wouldn't be able to directly donate to the party within the law.Electoral law states that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.Jukes appears to suggest that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.Elsewhere, James Orr, the party's head of policy suggests that the father could pay for opinion polling to support one of Reform's campaigns.Farage and Jukes were also filmed at a lunch in Clacton where it is suggested the US donor, who was being played by an actor, gives £500,000 to Reform through his son.Farage told the BBC he "frankly wasn't listening" to the discussion about the potential donation. Channel 4 News has said the payment was never made. He dismissed the comments made by his aide in the film as "loose pub talk including a couple of boasts that simply were not true".Jukes has denied "any wrongdoing" and said he had "stepped back from politics in order to clear my name".Last week, Orr told Sky News he would cooperate with the party's internal investigation "fully".The Met had already been investigating whether payments to Reform in the weeks before the last election complied with donation laws.The probe is examining donations given directly to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Nigel Farage ally, George Cottrell.It is also examining payments from a company controlled by Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice, which received £1m from Fiona Cottrell in June 2024.A Verbatim Investigations spokesperson said: "Verbatim will cooperate with the police's investigation."Labour Party Chair Bridget Phillipson said: "Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him."Reform's failure to take responsibility for their actions shows just how unfit they are for office."The Liberal Democrat's Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart said: "Every Reform MP urgently needs to state whether they or their campaigns have benefited from any foreign money."Zack Polanski, leader of the Green Party in England and Wales, said: "Nigel Farage and Lee Anderson hoped they could pin all this on two of their most senior advisors, but they have more questions to answer about how much they knew."

schema.headline: Police launch criminal investigation into Reform UK donations

title: Air traffic failure was avoidable, says transport secretary
description: A technical failure of the UK's air traffic control system that has caused widespread flight chaos was avoidable, according to the Transport Secretary
body: A technical failure of the UK's air traffic control system that has caused widespread flight chaos was avoidable, according to the Transport Secretary.  Heidi Alexander told the Commons she had ordered an independent investigation by the aviation watchdog into the system operated by Nats, which went down for four hours on Tuesday.More than 2,000 flights have been cancelled as disruption continued for a second day with passengers stuggling to fly out of and into the UK.After meeting with the boss of Nats, Martin Rolfe, Alexander said a cyberattack could be ruled out, but she added: "I do not believe this issue was unavoidable."Nats has apologised for its third major technical fault in three years.Alexander said she discussed with Rolfe how Nats, which is 49% owned by the government, "responded to resolve and minimise the disruption as quickly as possible".She said there had to be "tough questions about resilience of Nats systems", adding: "We also need to think about consumer redress issues."Earlier on Wednesday the government said it had confidence in Rolfe, who has led Nats for 11 years as airlines such as Wizz Air and Ryanair called for him to step down.Nats has been asked to investigate the incident and report back in one week. But Alexander said she has also asked the Civil Aviation Authority to conduct an independent review and present an update in six months' time.Airlines UK, which represents the country's carriers, said it had written to Alexander to "register serious concerns over yesterday's technical failure at Nats - the third major system failure in three years - which has caused major disruption across the UK's aviation network".Airlines UK's chief executive Tim Alderslade, said: "The result is a system where airlines pick up the bill for the mistakes of others, while the organisations responsible face little or no financial consequence."Accountability should sit where responsibility lies and the Civil Aviation Bill offers the opportunity to address this."The UK Civil Aviation Authority said passengers are unlikely to be entitled to compensation - though it reminded airlines of their responsibilities to look after passengers who flights had been delayed or cancelled.It added that the disruption caused by the Nats issue is "likely to be considered the result of 'extraordinary circumstances'", meaning passengers "are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident."Nats first confirmed it was investigating a "technical issue" at 13:46 BST on Tuesday, "which is causing some disruption to flight departures". The glitch occurred at Nats' Swanwick Centre in Hampshire, where one of its two air traffic control centres are. The other is in Prestwick, Ayrshire.Around 90 minutes later, it said it had identified that the issue was with its flight processing system.This processes flight plans and other operational information used by controllers to manage air traffic.It continually updates flight information as aircraft progress through UK airspace, helping controllers maintain a safe and orderly flow of traffic.By 19:30, Nats said the system issue had been resolved and it was working to clear the backlog of flights.However, by Wednesday evening, the number of flights that had been cancelled or failed to take off since the fault first emerged had grown to more than 2,000, according to flight analytics firm Cirium.According to tracking site FlightRadar24, the worst affected airports were Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Birmingham.A Heathrow spokesperson said on Wednesday its "operations are recovering"."Flights are operating today but we are expecting knock-on impacts as aircraft and crew reposition," it said.At Gatwick, a spokesperson said: "Flights have now resumed from London Gatwick. However, we still anticipate that it will take time for our operations to fully return to normal."Manchester, Luton, Stansted, Bristol, and Belfast City Airports all said on Wednesday that flights had resumed, though Bristol, Belfast and Luton said there continued to be knock-on effects.

schema.headline: Air traffic failure was avoidable, says transport secretary

title: Iran war won't end until after US midterm elections, says Trump
description: US President Donald Trump has said he does not think the Iran war will end until after November's midterm elections, adding that oil prices will not c
body: US President Donald Trump has said he does not think the Iran war will end until after November's midterm elections, adding that oil prices will not come down until then. "I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer," Trump said of Tehran on Wednesday.His comments come as he headed to Texas for the party's first convention ahead of the midterms, when the balance of power could change in the US government.Trump is facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war with Iran.On Wednesday, oil prices rose to $100 (£74) for the first time since July due to increased fighting in the Middle East."Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward," Trump told reporters. "I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm."He added that Iran was "desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there" - an apparent reference to the Democrats - "and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon". Tehran has repeatedly denied it is seeking nuclear weapons. Trump also said further negotiations with Iran could possibly happen, "but it's not something we're looking at".The US president initially predicted the war, which is now in its seventh month, would last only a matter of weeks. The conflict, and its knock-on effects on everything from gas to groceries, has led to a steep decline in his approval ratings.Fighting in the Middle East has intensified in recent days, as oil facilities throughout the region come under attack, driving up the global price of fuel and any item that requires shipping.On Wednesday, the US military said it had attacked five oil tanker ships with ties to Iran. Tehran, in response, launched attacks on two US Navy destroyers and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, causing "heavy damage" to the vessels, according to Iranian state media.A day earlier, the Iran-linked Houthis in Yemen launched a wave of attacks in Saudi Arabia, sparking fires at oil facilities.The fighting, which began again recently after a 60-day ceasefire between the US and Iran formally expired last month, has also raised predictions that the rising fuel costs could lead to higher interest rates in the US.

schema.headline: Iran war won't end until after US midterm elections, says Trump

title: Long Eaton school chaplain settles LGBT sermon unfair dismissal case
description: A chaplain who used a sermon to tell pupils they did not have to believe in "LGBT stuff" has reached a legal agreement with the school that dismissed
body: A chaplain who used a sermon to tell pupils they did not have to believe in "LGBT stuff" has reached a legal agreement with the school that dismissed him.Rev Bernard Randall was sacked by Trent College in Long Eaton, Derbyshire, in 2019, two months after the sermon. He appealed and his dismissal, external was overturned, but he was later made redundant after refusing reduced hours.After losing an unfair dismissal claim, his case had been set for a new tribunal over possible bias on the panel that made the ruling, and Trent College was ordered to pay Randall about £20,000 in costs, according to a court document.Advocacy group Christian Concern said a confidential settlement had since been reached.An employment tribunal heard Randall opposed parts of a programme the school was implementing to try to improve LGBT inclusivity.Randall told the tribunal he believed elements of the programme - devised by charity Educate and Celebrate - were Marxist, revolutionary, atheist and incompatible with Christian values.He said some of the terminology within the programme was "ideologically loaded and misleading", and he highlighted phrases such as "sex assigned at birth" and "cisgender".Randall told the tribunal: "Educate and Celebrate went beyond a neutral stance of inclusivity into the implantation of ideas I consider to be identity politics."He said he was inspired to write the sermon, delivered in June 2019 to pupils aged between 11 and 17, after he was asked by a sixth-form pupil: "Sir, how come we are told we have to accept all this LGBT stuff in a Christian school?"Randall included the question within the sermon, which he said concerned school leaders.He also said, in his sermon: "You do not have to accept the ideas of LGBT activists."Christian Concern said Randall's sermon reflected the Church of England's teaching on marriage, but it triggered complaints from some pupils, parents and staff members, who said it nearly left them in tears.Randall was removed from his role as chaplain at the fee-paying boarding school and reported to the government counter-terrorism watchdog Prevent.The Derby Telegraph reported, external Randall appealed against his dismissal, which was overturned, but he was given a final warning. Trent College then informed Randall it wanted to reduce the chaplaincy role to seven hours, term-time only, which he did not accept and was therefore made redundant. At an unfair dismissal hearing in February 2023, the judge said the school's redundancy process was genuine and reasonable, and the referral to Prevent had been justified "from a safeguarding perspective".Christian Concern said Bill Penty, the-then head of Trent College, then referred Randall to the Teaching Regulation Authority (TRA) and to the Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS).The TRA decided not to take forward a case, while the DBS ruled Randall had no case to answer, according to Christian Concern.In March 2025, Judge James Tayler, sitting in the Employment Appeal Tribunal, ruled the original judgment was "unsafe" and ordered the case be reheard, leading to the out-of-court settlement.Randall can also preach again in Church of England churches after, according to Christian Concern, an independent investigator said they could not "establish, on the balance of probabilities, that harm was caused by the delivery of the sermons".They concluded the "concern or allegation was unsubstantiated and there are no ongoing safeguarding concerns".Christian Concern said Randall had completed all mandatory safeguarding training and was now eligible for permission to officiate.Randall said "seven years have been taken from me" by the case and that his "faith and loyalty to the Church has been tested to the extreme".He added: "I encouraged pupils to think, to debate, and to love their neighbours whatever they believed."No minister, teacher or chaplain should be punished for upholding Christian teaching in a Christian setting."I want to thank my legal team and everyone who has stood with and supported me, and especially the many people who have prayed for me throughout this ordeal."Randall told the BBC he had "been out of ministry for over seven years" due to the case.He said: "I don't feel angry, I try not to. It's very difficult to forgive, I'm working on that."Trent College told the BBC it would not be making any further comment on the matter.

schema.headline: Long Eaton school chaplain settles LGBT sermon unfair dismissal case
